title: How Much Does Grab Bar Installation Cost in 2026?
meta_description: Grab bars cost about $100 to $400 each installed in 2026. See what tile, studs and bar style add, when DIY is risky, and which programs help pay for them.
short: Most people pay $200 to $350 per professionally installed grab bar, and tile or missing studs push the price up.
cost_drivers: Wall surface: porcelain, stone or fiberglass takes more time and special bits

faq.q: How much does it cost to have one grab bar installed?
faq.a: Plan on about $100 to $400 for one bar with labor. HomeGuide puts the total at $100 to $350 per bar, and Angi puts most professional installs at $200 to $350. Some pros charge a minimum visit fee, so one bar can cost almost as much as two.

faq.q: Does Medicare pay for grab bars?
faq.a: Original Medicare does not pay for grab bars or other home changes. Some Medicare Advantage plans offer a home safety benefit, so call your plan and ask before you buy.

faq.q: Can a grab bar go on a wall with no stud?
faq.a: Yes, but it needs the right hardware or a backing panel. Angi lists $100 to $200 per location for wall reinforcement or special anchors on weak or stud-free walls.

faq.q: Are towel bars safe to use as grab bars?
faq.a: No. Towel bars are not built to hold a person's weight. Use a bar sold as a grab bar and mount it into studs or with rated anchors.

body_md:
Grab bars are the cheapest safety change most homes can make. They help with the moments when falls happen: stepping out of a tub, standing up from a toilet, or turning in a wet shower.

This guide shows what people really pay in 2026, what makes one job cost more than another, and where to look for help paying.

## Grab bar cost at a glance

Two big cost guides agree that one installed bar usually runs a few hundred dollars. HomeGuide puts the bar plus labor at **$100 to $350 per bar** [1]. Angi says professional installs typically run **$200 to $350**, and lists a wider $100 to $400 range for hiring a pro [2]. Fixr's aging-in-place guide lands in the same zone at **$90 to $300** [3].

| Cost item | Typical price | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Bar plus installation, per bar | $100 – $350 | HomeGuide [1] |
| Professional install, per bar | $200 – $350 | Angi [2] |
| Bar only (straight) | $20 – $100 | Angi [2] |
| Fold-down bar (part only) | $50 – $280 | Angi [2] |
| Wall-to-floor bar (part only) | $80 – $250 | Angi [2] |
| Wall reinforcement, per spot | $100 – $400 | Angi [2] |
| Handyperson labor | $50 – $80 per hour | HomeGuide [1] |

Most homes need two to four bars, according to HomeGuide [1]. A common set is one by the toilet, one at the tub or shower entry, and one on the long shower wall. That puts a typical bathroom at roughly $400 to $1,400 for the set.

## What makes the price go up

### The wall behind the bar

The bar is only as strong as what holds it. On plain drywall with studs in the right place, a pro can mount a bar in 20 to 45 minutes [1]. Tile, fiberglass and stone take longer. Angi says these surfaces can add $100 to $150 in labor [2].

When studs are not where the bar needs to go, the installer may add blocking or a backing panel, or use rated anchors. Angi puts that work at $100 to $200 per location for simple cases, and up to $400 when more prep is needed [2]. If a wall cracks or a hole must be patched, HomeGuide warns drywall repair can run $300 to $1,500 or more [1].

### The type of bar

A straight bar is the low-cost choice. Angled bars, fold-down bars beside a toilet, and wall-to-floor poles cost more for the part alone [2]. Decorative finishes add about $50 per bar, and bars with a built-in shelf or towel rack add $30 to $200 [2].

### Small-job fees

Many contractors charge a service call fee for small jobs [1]. That is why it pays to have all bars put in during one visit.

## DIY or hire a pro?

You can find grab bars for under $100 at most hardware stores. Angi estimates a DIY cost of about $30 to $100 per bar if you already own tools [2].

The catch is safety. A grab bar has one job: hold a falling adult. If it is screwed only into drywall or into tile without proper anchors, it can rip out at the worst moment. Angi does not recommend DIY for complex walls, for people with limited mobility, or when the bar must meet ADA rules [2]. If you are not sure you hit a stud, hire a pro.

Grab bars rarely need a permit, because they do not change plumbing, wiring or structure. Check with your local building office if the job is part of a larger remodel.

## Who can help pay

Grab bars are cheap enough that many programs pay for them in full.

- **Area Agency on Aging.** Many local agencies fund small home safety repairs or can point you to a handyman program.
- **Nonprofit repair groups.** Groups such as Rebuilding Together often install grab bars for free for low-income older homeowners.
- **Medicaid waivers.** Home and community-based services waivers in many states cover home changes for people who qualify.
- **VA grants.** Veterans may qualify for the HISA grant for medically needed home changes.
- **USDA Section 504.** Rural homeowners 62 and older with very low income may get a repair grant that removes safety hazards.
- **Tax deduction.** The IRS lists railings, grab bars and bathroom changes made for a disability as medical expenses that usually do not add value to a home, so the full cost can count [4]. You can deduct only total medical costs above 7.5% of your adjusted gross income [4].

Original Medicare does not pay for physical home changes like grab bars [5]. Some Medicare Advantage plans include a home safety benefit, so call your plan before you pay out of pocket.

## Bottom line

Budget about $200 to $350 per bar for a pro to install it right, and more if your bathroom is tiled or lacks studs. Have every bar installed in one visit, and ask your local aging agency about free installs before you pay.

body_md:
Climbing over a tub wall is one of the riskiest things many older adults do each day. Replacing the tub with a walk-in shower removes that step. It is one of the most common aging-in-place projects.

Here is what it costs in 2026, and why prices vary so much.

## Tub-to-shower cost at a glance

The main cost guides agree on a broad range but not on the average.

- HomeGuide says most conversions cost **$2,000 to $12,000**, with a national average of about **$7,000** from member projects [1].
- This Old House gives the same **$2,000 to $12,000** range [3].
- Angi reports a much lower average of about **$3,000**, with a range of $1,200 to $15,000 [2].

The gap in averages likely reflects how many cheap kit jobs versus full tile jobs each site counts. Use the range, not one average, when you budget.

| Conversion type | Installed cost | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Tub cut (low step, tub stays) | $800 – $1,800 | HomeGuide [1] |
| Prefab shower stall | $1,000 – $8,000 | HomeGuide [1] |
| Prefab stall | $2,000 – $6,000 | This Old House [3] |
| Walk-in shower | $5,000 – $12,000 | This Old House [3] |
| Custom tile walk-in | $3,500 – $15,000 | HomeGuide [1], Angi [2] |
| Curbless (no lip) | $8,000 – $15,000 | This Old House [3] |

## What drives the price

### Kit or custom tile

A one-piece acrylic or fiberglass stall is the fastest and cheapest choice. The kit alone runs $350 to $4,100 [1]. Tile showers cost more because tile is labor-heavy, and a shower pan alone can run $500 to $3,500 [1].

### Plumbing changes

If the new shower drain sits where the tub drain was, costs stay down. Moving a drain runs about $900 to $1,100, and a new or upgraded shower valve about $700 to $1,200, according to This Old House [3]. Several plumbing changes can top $2,000 [3]. Some codes also call for a larger 2-inch shower drain in place of a 1.5-inch tub drain [1].

### Demolition and surprises

Tub removal and disposal runs $150 to $300 at Angi [2] and up to $1,200 at This Old House when more work is involved [3]. Old bathrooms often hide rot or mold under the tub. This Old House suggests setting aside 10 to 20 percent of the budget for surprises [3].

### Safety extras

A fold-down seat, a handheld shower head and grab bars make the shower safer. This Old House lists installed grab bars at $150 to $500 each and a fold-down seat at $300 to $800 [3]. Angi estimates basic safety features, a grab bar and seat, at about $600 [2].

## Size matters for safety

Most codes require a shower floor of at least about 30 by 30 inches [1]. For someone who uses a walker or needs a helper, bigger is better. Angi lists an ADA-size 36 by 36 stall at $1,300 to $5,500 [2].

If a one-piece stall is planned, measure your bathroom door first. HomeGuide warns that one-piece units must fit through the doorway [1].

## DIY or hire a pro?

Angi says doing some of the work yourself can save $1,000 or more [2]. Good DIY tasks are tub removal, painting and simple fixture swaps. Plumbing mistakes, though, can cost hundreds to thousands to fix [2]. This Old House recommends a pro for moving plumbing, changing valves, custom tile or subfloor work [3].

Permits are often needed when plumbing moves. HomeGuide lists $30 to $400 [1], while Angi lists $200 to $2,000 [2]. Fees vary a lot by town.

## Who can help pay

- **Area Agency on Aging** and **nonprofit repair groups** may fund or build a safer shower for low-income seniors.
- **Medicaid waivers** in many states cover bathroom changes for people who qualify for home care.
- **VA grants** such as HISA can cover a roll-in or walk-in shower for eligible veterans.
- **USDA Section 504** loans and grants help very-low-income rural owners fix safety hazards.
- **City or county CDBG** and **state housing finance agency** repair programs sometimes fund accessible bathrooms.
- **Tax deduction:** bathroom changes made for a disability can count as medical expenses under IRS rules when they do not add home value.

## Bottom line

Budget $2,000 to $6,000 for a basic prefab conversion and $5,000 to $12,000 or more for tile. Keep the drain in place, add a seat and grab bars, and get at least three written quotes.

title: How Much Does a Curbless Roll-In Shower Cost in 2026?
meta_description: A curbless roll-in shower costs about $2,900 to $15,000 in 2026, and sources disagree widely. See why, what drives the price, and who helps pay for one.
short: Roll-in showers range from about $2,900 for a prefab base to $15,000 or more for a custom tiled curbless shower.

faq.q: Why do roll-in shower prices vary so much?
faq.a: A prefab roll-in base set into an existing shower space is a modest job. A custom tiled shower with a recessed floor and new drain is a full remodel. Angi reports an average of $3,800, while This Old House lists curbless showers at $8,000 to $15,000.

faq.q: Is a curbless shower more expensive than a regular walk-in shower?
faq.a: Usually somewhat. Angi says to expect about $500 to $700 more than a standard walk-in shower. Fixr says going curbless often does not add much.

faq.q: Does the VA pay for roll-in showers?

faq.q: What size should a roll-in shower be?

body_md:
A curbless, or roll-in, shower has no lip at the entry. A wheelchair, shower chair or walker can roll straight in. It is the gold standard for bathroom access, and it is often the change that lets someone stay home after a stroke or major surgery.

Prices vary more for this project than almost any other on our site. Here is why, and how to budget.

## Roll-in shower cost at a glance

The sources we checked disagree, and we are showing that disagreement instead of hiding it.

- **Angi** reports a national average of **$3,800**, with most jobs between **$2,900 and $4,600**, plus $250 to $1,000 for permits, cleanup and demolition [1].
- **This Old House** lists curbless showers at **$8,000 to $15,000** when replacing a tub [2].
- **Fixr** puts walk-in showers at **$5,000 to $11,000** on average, with custom 60 by 60 curbless builds reaching **$20,000 or more** [3].

The low numbers mostly reflect prefab roll-in bases put into a space already sized for a shower. The high numbers reflect custom tile, a recessed floor and new plumbing.

| Scenario | Typical installed cost | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Existing shower already ADA size, add roll-in base, bench, rails | About $1,300 in parts plus labor | Angi [1] |
| Standard roll-in shower | $2,900 – $4,600 | Angi [1] |
| Prefab walk-in shower | $2,000 – $8,000 | Fixr [3] |
| Custom walk-in shower | $5,000 – $20,000 | Fixr [3] |
| Curbless shower replacing a tub | $8,000 – $15,000 | This Old House [2] |

## Why curbless costs more than a standard shower

Water must stay in the shower without a curb to stop it. That means the floor must slope toward the drain, and in many homes the shower area must be lowered so the floor stays level with the rest of the bathroom. Angi says curbless showers often cost **$500 to $700 more** than standard walk-in showers, and more in a full wet-room design where the whole room is waterproofed [4]. Fixr, by contrast, says going curbless "doesn't usually add much" [3]. Expect the extra cost to depend on your floor.

### Size

Angi prices common roll-in sizes from about $2,600 for a 60 by 30 inch shower to $3,600 for 63 by 39 inches in materials [1]. A wheelchair user who needs a helper often benefits from the larger end.

### Plumbing and floors

Moving the drain and supply lines adds $200 to $500 in plumber labor at Fixr [3], or $900 to $1,100 just to move a drain at This Old House [2]. Concrete slabs and floor joists can make recessing the floor harder.

### Safety features

Most roll-in showers also need a fold-down seat, grab bars, a handheld shower on a slide bar and controls the seated user can reach. Fixr lists grab bars at $85 to $300 each and a bench at $100 to $500 [3].

## Timing

Angi says an average install takes two to four days, but jobs that need demolition or new plumbing can stretch much longer [1]. Plan temporary bathing, such as a sponge bath or a second bathroom, during the work.

## DIY or hire a pro?

This is a job for a licensed contractor. Angi advises against DIY roll-in showers because of water damage and safety risks [1]. Ask for a contractor who has built curbless showers before, and ask how they will slope and waterproof the floor. A Certified Aging-in-Place Specialist (CAPS) or an occupational therapist can help with layout.

Most areas require a permit when plumbing is moved. Angi lists about $250 per permit [1], and Fixr says $100 to $500 [3].

## Who can help pay

- **VA HISA grant.** The VA lists roll-in showers as a covered bathroom change. The lifetime grant is $6,800 for a service-connected disability (or a non-service-connected one if rated 50 percent or more) and $2,000 for others [5]. Larger VA housing grants exist for severe service-connected disabilities.
- **Medicaid waivers** often cover accessible showers for people who qualify for home care.
- **Area Agency on Aging**, **Centers for Independent Living** and **nonprofit repair groups** can help find funding or crews.
- **USDA Section 504**, **city CDBG** and **state housing finance agency** programs fund repairs for income-eligible owners.
- **Tax deduction.** Bathroom changes for a disability can count as a medical expense when they do not add home value.

## Bottom line

Budget about $3,000 to $5,000 if a prefab roll-in base fits your existing shower space, and $8,000 to $15,000 for a custom curbless shower that replaces a tub. Get an assessment first so the shower fits the person who will use it.

title: How Much Does a Walk-In Tub Cost in 2026?
meta_description: Walk-in tubs cost about $3,500 to $10,000 installed for most buyers in 2026, and luxury models top $25,000. See price drivers, hidden costs and funding help.
short: Most walk-in tubs cost $4,000 to $10,000 installed, but jets, brand and water heater upgrades can push them past $20,000.

Electrical work for jets, heated seats and pumps

Fast-fill faucet and quick-drain options

faq.q: What is the average cost of a walk-in tub?
faq.a: Fixr puts the national average at about $6,000 installed, with most jobs between $3,500 and $10,000. HomeGuide lists standard tubs at $4,000 to $18,000 installed.

faq.q: Does Medicare pay for a walk-in tub?
faq.a: Original Medicare does not cover walk-in tubs. Some Medicare Advantage plans may offer partial help, and Medicaid waivers in some states cover bathroom changes.

faq.q: Will I need a new water heater?
faq.a: Possibly. Walk-in tubs hold a lot of water. Fixr lists a point-of-use heater at $300 to $1,000, and HomeGuide lists water heater replacement at $1,400 to $5,600.

faq.q: Is a walk-in shower a better choice?
faq.a: For many people, yes. A walk-in shower often costs less, and you do not have to sit inside while the tub fills and drains. A walk-in tub suits people who want to soak or need warm water therapy.

body_md:
A walk-in tub has a door in the side and a built-in seat. You step over a low sill, close the door, and sit while the tub fills. It suits people who love to soak or who get relief from warm water, but it is one of the pricier bathroom changes.

Here is what walk-in tubs cost in 2026.

## Walk-in tub cost at a glance

- **Fixr** reports a national average of **$6,000** installed, with most jobs between **$3,500 and $10,000** [1].
- **HomeGuide** lists standard tubs at **$4,000 to $18,000** installed, and high-end or complex jobs at **$8,000 to $25,000 or more** [2].
- **Forbes Health** lists tubs from about **$2,000 to $20,000** before installation, and quotes a contractor who puts installation at **$2,000 to $10,000** [3].

So sources agree on the starting point but not on the top. Luxury and two-person tubs drive the high end.

| Tub type | Price | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Soaker | $3,000 – $7,000 | Fixr [1] |
| Hydrotherapy or whirlpool | $4,000 – $12,000 | Fixr [1] |
| Bariatric | $4,500 – $11,500 | Fixr [1] |
| Wheelchair accessible | $4,500 – $12,000 | Fixr [1] |
| Two-seat | $6,000 – $20,000 | Fixr [1] |
| Luxury | $8,000 – $30,000+ | Fixr [1] |
| Installation labor | $1,000 – $3,500 | Fixr [1] |

## Hidden costs to ask about

The tub itself is only part of the bill.

### Hot water

A walk-in tub holds far more water than a standard tub. If your water heater is small, the bath may run cool. Fixr lists a point-of-use heater at $300 to $1,000 [1]. HomeGuide lists full water heater replacement at $1,400 to $5,600 installed [2].

### Wiring

Jets, pumps and heated seats need power. Electricians charge about $50 to $130 per hour [2]. Some tubs need a dedicated circuit near the tub.

### Plumbing, walls and floors

Forbes Health lists add-on costs that can stack up: drain or pipe work at $250 to $2,500, wall repair at $1,000 to $5,000, and flooring at $500 to $3,500 [3]. HomeGuide lists plumbing upgrades at $350 to $2,000 [2].

### Features

A fast-fill faucet ($150 to $500) and a rapid-release drain ($200 to $400) shorten the time you sit in a cooling tub [1]. Massage jets can add $3,000 to $8,000 [1].

## Things to know before you buy

You must get in before the tub fills and wait for it to drain before you open the door. For someone who gets cold easily, a fast drain and a heated seat matter.

Inward-swinging doors are common on lower-priced tubs, Forbes notes [3]. Outward doors can be easier for some users. Check the step-in height and the seat height against the person who will use it.

Many walk-in tubs are sold in home by dealers. Get written quotes from more than one company, and do not sign the same day.

## DIY or hire a pro?

Hire a pro. Installation usually takes one to two days [2]. Fixr says a simple swap may not need a permit, but significant plumbing or electrical changes can mean permits of $150 to $1,000 [1]. Ask the installer who pulls the permit.

## Who can help pay

- **Medicare:** Original Medicare does not cover walk-in tubs [2] [3]. Some Medicare Advantage plans may offer partial coverage [1].
- **Medicaid waivers:** Coverage varies by state. Forbes notes that Colorado's Elderly, Blind and Disabled waiver covers some bathroom changes [3].
- **VA:** The HISA grant can help veterans with medically needed bathroom changes [1].
- **USDA Section 504:** Rural homeowners 62 and older with very low income may get a grant of up to $10,000 [1].
- **Nonprofit repair groups** such as Rebuilding Together, plus local aging agencies and city CDBG programs, may help [1] [2].
- **Tax deduction:** If a doctor prescribes it, the tub may count as a medical expense. Only medical costs above 7.5 percent of adjusted gross income are deductible [3].

## Bottom line

Budget $4,000 to $10,000 for a mid-range tub, and ask early about hot water, wiring and wall repair. If soaking is not the main goal, price a walk-in shower too.

diy: A raised seat is a simple DIY install. Replacing a toilet is a common DIY job too, but a bad wax seal can leak into the floor. If the floor is soft or the flange is broken, hire a plumber.

faq.q: How tall is a comfort-height toilet?
faq.a: Comfort-height toilets put the seat about 17 to 19 inches above the floor, compared with about 14.5 to 16 inches for standard toilets, according to Angi.

faq.q: Does Medicare pay for a raised toilet seat?
faq.a: Generally no. CMS's DME list has long treated raised toilet seats as convenience items. Medicare Part B does cover a commode chair when it is medically needed and prescribed for home use.

faq.q: Is a comfort-height toilet more expensive?
faq.a: Not by much. This Old House says they cost about $50 to $100 more than standard models. Angi notes prices are close and installation costs about the same.

faq.q: Raised seat or new toilet: which is better?
faq.a: A raised seat is cheap and fast, and good for short-term needs such as hip surgery recovery. A comfort-height toilet is sturdier, looks normal and does not shift, so it is better for the long term.

body_md:
Getting up from a low toilet is hard on knees and hips. A few extra inches of height can make a big difference. You have two main options: add a raised seat to the toilet you have, or replace it with a comfort-height toilet.

Here is what each one costs in 2026.

## Cost at a glance

| Option | Typical cost | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Raised toilet seat with arms (retail) | About $47 – $54 | Retail listings [4] [5] |
| Comfort-height upcharge vs. standard toilet | $50 – $100 more | This Old House [2] |
| Installation, either height | About $375 | Angi [1] |
| Full toilet replacement with a plumber | $500 – $800 | This Old House [2] |
| Comfort-height toilet, installed range | $100 – $1,600 | Fixr [3] |

## Option 1: a raised toilet seat

A raised seat sits on top of your toilet bowl and adds a few inches of height. Many come with padded arms to push up from.

We checked two retail listings in October 2026. A Carex raised seat with removable padded arms that adds 3.5 inches of height and holds 250 pounds sold for **$54.37** [4]. A similar Carex elevated seat with arms was **$46.79** at a pharmacy [5].

Raised seats are a good fit for short-term needs, such as recovery from hip or knee surgery. Downsides: some shift when you sit, they can be hard to clean, and others in the house may not like them.

## Option 2: a comfort-height toilet

A comfort-height, or chair-height, toilet is built taller. Angi says the seat sits about **17 to 19 inches** from the floor, compared with about **14.5 to 16 inches** for standard toilets [1]. That puts it in the range ADA guidelines use for adults [1].

### Toilet price

This Old House says comfort-height models cost about **$50 to $100 more** than standard models, and that a mid-range toilet runs about $375 to $500 [2]. Angi says prices for the two heights are close [1].

### Installation

Angi puts installation at about **$375** for either height [1]. This Old House lists full replacement with a plumber at **$500 to $800**, and ground-floor installs with existing plumbing at $350 to $500 [2]. Removing the old toilet can add $50 to $200 [2].

Fixr's aging-in-place guide lists a wider **$100 to $1,600** for a comfort-height toilet [3]. The top of that range covers premium models and jobs with extra work.

## What can raise the price

- **Floor or flange damage.** When the old toilet comes up, the plumber may find a broken flange or soft floor. This Old House lists medium floor damage at $200 to $500 and subfloor repair at $500 to $1,500 [2].
- **Features.** A bidet seat adds $100 to $500, and a soft-close lid $30 to $75 [2].
- **Grab bars.** This Old House lists wheelchair-friendly grab bars at $100 to $300 [2]. A bar or toilet safety frame next to the toilet often matters as much as height.

## DIY or hire a pro?

Anyone can put on a raised seat in a few minutes. Follow the maker's directions and check that it locks tight.

Swapping a toilet is a common DIY job. The savings are mostly the labor and removal fee [2]. The risk is a slow leak under the toilet that rots the floor. If you are not confident, hire a plumber. A permit is not usually needed for a like-for-like toilet swap, but check with your town.

## Who can help pay

- **Medicare:** CMS's durable medical equipment list has long classed raised toilet seats and grab bars as not primarily medical, so they are not covered [6]. Medicare Part B does cover a **commode chair** as medical equipment when a provider prescribes it for home use. You pay 20 percent after the Part B deductible [7].
- **Area Agency on Aging** and **nonprofit repair groups** often supply raised seats or install toilets for low-income seniors.
- **State assistive technology programs** may lend or give used equipment such as raised seats.
- **Medicaid waivers** and **VA** programs can cover bathroom changes for people who qualify.
- **Tax deduction:** home changes for a disability can count as medical expenses under IRS rules.

## Bottom line

Start with a $50 raised seat if the need is short-term. For the long term, a comfort-height toilet costs only a little more than a standard one and usually runs $375 to $800 installed.

title: How Much Does a Straight Stair Lift Cost in 2026?
meta_description: A straight stair lift costs about $2,000 to $9,000 installed in 2026, and used units start near $1,500. See what drives price, rental costs and who helps pay.
short: New straight stair lifts usually cost $2,000 to $9,000 installed; used lifts and rentals can cut the cost for short-term needs.
cost_drivers: New versus used or refurbished
Staircase length
Battery versus hardwired power
Seat type (swivel, perch, powered footrest) and weight capacity
Indoor versus outdoor model
New outlet, circuit or drywall repair
diy: Not recommended. HomeGuide notes the Accessibility Equipment Manufacturer's Association does not support DIY installs. A poorly mounted rail can fail under load, and DIY can void the warranty.

faq.q: What is the average cost of a straight stair lift?
faq.a: Angi puts the average installed straight lift at about $7,050, within a $2,000 to $9,000 range. HomeGuide lists $2,000 to $8,500. HomeAdvisor's accessibility guide lists a lower $1,500 to $5,000.

faq.q: Does Medicare cover stair lifts?
faq.a: No. Original Medicare treats stair lifts as home changes, not medical equipment. Some Medicare Advantage plans may help if a doctor prescribes one.

faq.q: Can I rent a stair lift?
faq.a: Yes, usually for straight stairs only. Angi lists rentals at $300 to $500 a month, plus a $500 to $1,000 deposit and install and removal fees. HomeGuide says renting rarely pays off unless the need is short.

faq.q: How long does installation take?
faq.a: HomeGuide says a straight lift takes about 2 to 6 hours to install.

body_md:
A stair lift is a motorized chair that rides a rail along your stairs. For many families it is the change that keeps an upstairs bedroom usable. Straight staircases, with no turns or landings, are the cheapest to fit.

Here is what a straight stair lift costs in 2026.

## Straight stair lift cost at a glance

The major guides overlap but do not match.

- **Angi:** **$2,000 to $9,000** for a straight lift, with an average installed straight lift of about **$7,050** [2].
- **HomeGuide:** **$2,000 to $8,500** installed [1].
- **HomeAdvisor:** **$1,500 to $5,000** for stair or chair lift installation [3].

HomeAdvisor's lower figures stand out. They may reflect more basic or used units. Do not count on the low end without a written quote.

| Option | Typical cost | Source |
|---|---|---|
| New straight lift, installed | $2,000 – $8,500 | HomeGuide [1] |
| New straight lift, installed | $2,000 – $9,000 | Angi [2] |
| Used or refurbished lift | $1,500 – $3,000 | Angi [2] |
| Outdoor lift | $3,500 – $12,000 | HomeGuide [1] |
| Rental | $300 – $500 per month | Angi [2] |
| Yearly maintenance | $100 – $300 | HomeGuide [1] |

## What drives the price

### Power source

Battery-powered lifts charge at the ends of the rail and keep working in a power outage. Angi lists battery models at **$3,000 to $5,000** and hardwired electric models at **$4,000 to $9,000**, and says battery models run about 30 to 40 percent cheaper [2].

### Seat and features

Swivel seats help you get off safely at the top. Perch seats suit people who cannot bend their knees. Angi lists add-ons such as a seat belt upgrade ($50 to $150), obstruction sensors ($100 to $400) and powered footrests or armrests ($50 to $200) [2].

### Weight capacity

Standard lifts carry about 300 to 400 pounds. Heavy-duty models carry about 400 to 600 pounds and cost more [1].

### Electrical and wall work

A lift may need a new outlet ($150 to $350) or a dedicated circuit ($250 to $900), plus $300 to $500 for drywall patching [1].

## Used and rental lifts

A used lift can save thousands, but Angi notes it only works if it fits your stairs [2]. Straight rails are easier to reuse than curved ones. Ask for a warranty on any used unit.

Renting runs **$150 to $500 a month** at HomeGuide [1] and $300 to $500 at Angi [2]. Expect a $500 to $1,000 deposit, plus install and removal fees of $400 to $700 and $300 to $600 at Angi [2]. HomeGuide says renting usually only makes sense for a short need, such as surgery recovery [1].

## Upkeep

HomeGuide puts yearly maintenance at **$100 to $300**, and some makers require a yearly inspection to keep the warranty [1]. Ask what the warranty covers and how fast the dealer responds to a breakdown.

## DIY or hire a pro?

Hire a trained installer. HomeGuide says DIY installation is risky, and the Accessibility Equipment Manufacturer's Association does not support it [1]. Installation of a straight lift takes about 2 to 6 hours [1]. Angi notes a permit may be needed in some places [2].

## Who can help pay

- **Medicare:** Original Medicare does not cover stair lifts, because they count as home changes, not medical equipment [1] [2]. Some Medicare Advantage plans may help with a doctor's prescription [1].
- **Medicaid waivers:** A state home and community-based services waiver may pay, depending on state rules [1].
- **VA:** The VA may cover stair lifts for eligible veterans with service-related disabilities [1].
- **Nonprofits and aging agencies:** Groups such as Rebuilding Together and Area Agencies on Aging may offer grants or help finding funds [1].
- **State assistive technology programs** sometimes offer low-interest loans or reused equipment.
- **Tax deduction:** HomeGuide says a stair lift may be deductible as a medical expense when a provider documents that it is medically necessary [1]. IRS rules count only medical costs above 7.5 percent of adjusted gross income [4].

## Bottom line

Budget $3,000 to $7,000 for a new straight lift from a reputable dealer. Ask about battery power, a swivel seat and the warranty, and consider a used or rental unit if the need is short.

title: How Much Does a Curved Stair Lift Cost in 2026?
meta_description: Curved stair lifts cost about $9,000 to $20,000 installed in 2026, and long or complex stairs reach $30,000. See why custom rails cost more and who helps pay.
short: Curved stair lifts need a custom rail and usually cost $9,000 to $20,000 installed, with an average near $13,000.
cost_drivers: Custom-built rail measured to your exact stairs
Number of steps, turns and landings
Seat options such as a power swivel
Electrical outlet or dedicated circuit
Hard-to-reach installs and drywall repair
diy: No. Curved rails are custom-made for one staircase and must be installed by a trained technician. Used curved rails rarely fit another home.

faq.q: Why are curved stair lifts so much more expensive?
faq.a: Each curved rail is built to fit one staircase. The design, bending and fitting add cost, and the rail usually cannot be reused in another home.

faq.q: How much does a curved stair lift cost per step?
faq.a: Angi prices by staircase size: about $9,000 to $12,000 for 10 to 14 steps, rising to $20,000 to $30,000 for 30 or more steps.

faq.q: How long does it take to get a curved stair lift?
faq.a: Angi says the custom rail can take several weeks to build, and installation itself takes one to two days.

faq.q: Can I buy a used curved stair lift?
faq.a: Rarely in a useful way, because the rail is shaped for someone else's stairs. Some dealers reuse the chair and build a new rail, which can trim the cost.

body_md:
If your stairs turn, have a landing in the middle or curve, a standard straight lift will not work. You need a curved stair lift with a rail built for your staircase. That custom work is why these lifts cost several times more than straight ones.

## Curved stair lift cost at a glance

- **Angi's curved lift guide** lists a typical range of **$9,000 to $30,000**, with an average of about **$13,000** [1]. Its summary box gives $9,000 to $20,000, so the top of the range depends on which part of the page you read.
- **Angi's main stair lift guide** lists curved lifts at **$10,350 to $25,000** [2].
- **HomeGuide** lists curved lifts, or straight stairs with a landing, at **$7,500 to $15,000 or more** [3].

HomeGuide's range sits lower than Angi's. Most families should plan for low-to-mid teens and expect more for long or complex stairs.

| Staircase size | Typical installed cost | Source |
|---|---|---|
| 10 – 14 steps | $9,000 – $12,000 | Angi [1] |
| 15 – 19 steps | $12,000 – $15,000 | Angi [1] |
| 20 – 24 steps | $15,000 – $18,000 | Angi [1] |
| 25 – 29 steps | $18,000 – $20,000 | Angi [1] |
| 30+ steps | $20,000 – $30,000 | Angi [1] |

## What drives the price

### The custom rail

The rail is the main cost. A technician measures your stairs, often with photos or a 3D survey, and a factory bends a rail to match. Angi lists custom rail work at $1,000 to $5,000 within the total [1]. More turns and tight landings mean more cost.

### Seat and safety options

Angi lists a power swivel seat at $500 to $1,000, a battery backup at $200 to $600, a larger seat or footrest at $300 to $500, and custom upholstery at $200 to $800 [1].

### Electrical and finish work

Many lifts need an outlet near the top or bottom. Angi lists an outlet at $100 to $450 and a dedicated circuit at $570 to $1,000 [1]. Drywall repair can add $300 to $900, and hard-to-reach installs $500 to $1,500 [1].

## Permits

Angi lists an electrical permit at **$75 to $200** and a building permit for minor structural work at **$150 to $500** [1]. Your dealer should tell you whether your town requires either.

## Timing

Angi says the custom rail can take several weeks to make, and installation then takes one to two days [1]. If someone is coming home from the hospital soon, ask about a temporary plan, such as a first-floor bed, while you wait.

## Lifespan and upkeep

Angi says a curved lift lasts about 7 to 15 years with proper care, and recommends a yearly inspection [1]. Ask the dealer for the yearly service price before you sign.

## Ways to lower the cost

- Get quotes from at least three dealers. Prices for the same stairs can vary by thousands.
- Ask whether a straight lift could work with a short extension, or whether a landing could be handled with two straight lifts. Sometimes it is cheaper, sometimes not.
- Ask about refurbished chairs on a new rail. Angi notes refurbished lifts cost less, without giving a figure [1].
- Compare with a vertical platform lift or home elevator only if a wheelchair is involved, since those cost more.

## DIY or hire a pro?

Hire a pro. The rail is engineered for your stairs, and installation affects safety and warranty.

## Who can help pay

- **Medicare:** Angi notes Medicare does not cover stair lifts [2].
- **Medicaid, VA and HUD programs:** Angi lists Medicaid, the VA, TRICARE and HUD-funded programs as possible sources [2]. HomeGuide adds that a state Medicaid HCBS waiver may pay depending on state rules [3].
- **Nonprofits and Area Agencies on Aging** may offer grants or point you to funds [3].
- **State assistive technology programs** may offer low-interest loans.
- **Tax deduction:** HomeGuide says a stair lift may be deductible when prescribed, with written proof it is medically necessary [3]. Only medical costs above 7.5 percent of adjusted gross income count [4].

## Bottom line

Plan on $9,000 to $20,000 for most curved stairs, and more for long or complex ones. Compare several written quotes, ask about lead time, and check funding before you sign.

title: How Much Does a Vertical Platform (Porch) Lift Cost in 2026?
meta_description: A vertical platform or porch lift costs about $5,000 to $20,000 installed in 2026, and sources disagree widely. See price drivers, ramp vs lift and funding.
short: Wheelchair porch lifts usually cost $5,000 to $20,000 installed, depending on height, enclosure and outdoor build.
cost_drivers: Lifting height and number of stops
Open porch lift versus enclosed or shaftway model
Outdoor weatherproofing
Platform size and weight capacity
Concrete pad, electrical work and powered gates
diy: No. Platform lifts carry a person in a wheelchair and must be installed and inspected to code by a trained technician. Many areas require a permit and inspection.

faq.q: Is a porch lift cheaper than a ramp?
faq.a: Not usually for short rises. Angi lists ramps at $100 to $250 per linear foot, so a short ramp often costs less. For high porches, a ramp may need to be very long, and a lift can be the better fit.

faq.q: Does Medicare pay for a wheelchair porch lift?
faq.a: Original Medicare does not cover residential wheelchair lifts. Some Medicare Advantage plans may help.

faq.q: Does the VA pay for platform lifts?
faq.a: VA health care may cover a platform lift for eligible veterans with a service-connected disability. Note that the VA HISA grant lists porch lifts as removable equipment it does not cover, so the funding comes through other VA channels.

faq.q: Is a porch lift tax deductible?
faq.a: IRS Publication 502 lists porch lifts and other lifts among disability home changes that generally do not add home value, so the full cost can count as a medical expense.

body_md:
A vertical platform lift, often called a porch lift, raises a person in a wheelchair straight up from the ground to a porch or deck. It takes much less space than a long ramp. Some models also work indoors between split levels.

Prices vary widely, and the sources we checked do not agree. Here is the full picture.

## Platform lift cost at a glance

- **RetirementLiving.com** puts residential vertical platform lifts at **$9,000 to $20,000** with installation [1].
- **Angi** lists vertical platform lifts at **$5,000 to $20,000** in its home elevator guide [2].
- **HomeGuide** lists wheelchair platform lifts at **$4,000 to $15,000 or more** [3].
- **Angi's** home accessibility guide lists porch or patio lifts much lower, at **$2,000 to $6,000** [4].
- **PayingForSeniorCare** says a basic vertical platform lift runs about **$5,000** with installation, and lists installation alone at $1,000 to $4,000. That page was last updated in 2021 [5].

The low figures likely describe short, basic outdoor lifts. The high figures include taller or enclosed lifts. Get a site visit and written quote before you budget.

| Lift type | Typical cost | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Basic porch or patio lift | $2,000 – $6,000 | Angi [4] |
| Wheelchair platform lift | $4,000 – $15,000+ | HomeGuide [3] |
| Vertical platform lift | $5,000 – $20,000 | Angi [2] |
| Residential VPL, installed | $9,000 – $20,000 | RetirementLiving [1] |

## What drives the price

### Height

RetirementLiving says lifts that travel higher or serve more than one landing cost more [1]. A lift that clears three steps is a very different machine from one that reaches a second-floor deck.

### Open or enclosed

Open porch lifts are at the low end of the range. Enclosed or shaftway models with more features are at the high end [1]. Enclosed models also take longer to install, from several days to weeks, compared with about a day for an open porch lift [1].

### Outdoor build

Outdoor lifts must handle rain, heat and cold, which adds cost [1]. Many need a concrete base [1]. Plan for that pad in your budget if your yard does not have one.

### Size, capacity and controls

A wider platform, higher weight limit and powered gates or automatic controls all add cost [1]. A standard platform has a clear area of about 4 by 5 feet [1].

## Ramp or lift?

A ramp has no motor to break and works in a power outage. Angi lists ramps at **$100 to $250 per linear foot** [6]. A common rule is one foot of ramp for each inch of rise, so a 30-inch porch needs about 30 feet of ramp plus landings. When the porch is high or the yard is small, a lift can fit where a ramp cannot.

## Permits and upkeep

Platform lifts are regulated in many states, and a permit and inspection are often required. Ask your installer who pulls the permit and whether a yearly inspection is needed. RetirementLiving says regular checks and maintenance are needed but gives no price [1], so ask for a written service quote.

## DIY or hire a pro?

Hire a trained lift installer. These machines carry a person and chair several feet in the air.

## Who can help pay

- **Medicare:** Original Medicare does not cover residential wheelchair lifts. Some Medicare Advantage plans may [5].
- **Medicaid waivers:** Home and community-based services waivers may cover a platform lift as a home change, though funding is limited [5].
- **VA:** VA health care may cover a platform lift for eligible veterans with a service-related disability [5]. The VA's HISA grant itself lists porch lifts as removable equipment it does not cover [7], so ask your VA Prosthetic and Sensory Aids Service which program applies.
- **Centers for Independent Living** and **state assistive technology programs** can help compare options and find loans.
- **Tax deduction:** The IRS lists porch lifts and other lifts among disability changes that usually do not raise home value, so the full reasonable cost can count as a medical expense [8].

## Bottom line

Budget $5,000 to $20,000, with short, open outdoor lifts at the low end. Price a ramp too, and get at least two site visits before choosing.

diy: No. Home elevators must be installed by licensed elevator professionals, and most states require permits and inspections.

faq.q: What is the cheapest type of home elevator?
faq.a: Shaftless, through-the-floor models are usually the lowest-cost true elevators. Angi lists them at $15,000 to $25,000, and HomeGuide at $30,000 to $50,000. Both serve only two floors.

faq.q: How much does each extra floor add?
faq.a: HomeGuide says each added floor adds $10,000 to $15,000. Angi gives $5,000 to $15,000.

faq.q: What does a home elevator cost to maintain?
faq.a: Angi lists a yearly maintenance contract at $200 to $350 and a yearly inspection at $75 to $300. HomeGuide lists inspections at $150 to $700.

faq.q: Is a home elevator tax deductible?

body_md:
A home elevator lets someone reach every floor without stairs, even in a wheelchair. It is the most expensive aging-in-place change on our list, but for a multi-story home it can cost less than moving.

## Home elevator cost at a glance

- **HomeGuide** puts most two-story installs at **$30,000 to $60,000**, with a national average of **$48,000** and a range of $20,000 to $100,000 [1].
- **Angi** lists elevators by type from **$15,000** (shaftless) to **$60,000** (pneumatic) [2].

Angi's page also shows an overall national average of about $4,191, which is far below its own by-type prices. That figure appears to blend in small lift jobs, so we do not use it for elevators. The by-type numbers from both sites line up much better.

| Elevator type | HomeGuide [1] | Angi [2] |
|---|---|---|
| Shaftless / through-the-floor | $30,000 – $50,000 | $15,000 – $25,000 |
| Cable or winding drum | $28,000 – $50,000 | $15,000 – $35,000 |
| Hydraulic | $30,000 – $60,000 | $25,000 – $50,000 |
| Geared traction | $30,000 – $60,000 | $25,000 – $38,000 |
| Gearless traction | $50,000 – $75,000 | $29,000 – $55,000 |
| Pneumatic (vacuum) | $35,000 – $100,000 | $35,000 – $60,000 |
| Glass | $50,000 – $100,000+ | — |

The two sites disagree most on shaftless models. Get quotes from at least two brands.

## What drives the price

### Shaft or no shaft

A traditional elevator needs a shaft, a pit below it and sometimes a machine room [1]. HomeGuide says that construction takes about 4 to 5 weeks on average [1]. Shaftless models skip the pit and shaft, need 1 to 3 weeks of prep, and are easier to fit into an existing home [1]. They are usually limited to two floors [2].

### Floors served

Each extra floor adds **$10,000 to $15,000** at HomeGuide [1] and **$5,000 to $15,000** at Angi [2].

### Retrofit versus new build

Angi says retrofitting an existing home can cost up to three times more than installing during new construction [2]. A stacked set of closets can make a good path for the shaft and save money [1].

### Electrical and structural work

HomeGuide lists a dedicated circuit at $250 to $900 and an electrical panel upgrade at $1,300 to $4,000 [1]. Moving walls, plumbing or ducts adds more.

### Finishes

Cab finishes, automatic doors and custom controls all raise the price. Angi notes automatic or decorative doors can add up to $25,000 [2].

## Permits, inspection and upkeep

- **Permits:** $300 to $2,000 at HomeGuide [1]; $200 to $2,000 at Angi [2].
- **Inspection:** Most states require a yearly inspection by a licensed elevator technician, HomeGuide says, at about $150 to $700 [1]. Angi lists $75 to $300 [2].
- **Maintenance:** Angi lists a yearly contract at $200 to $350 [2]. Cable-driven models need new cables every 3 to 5 years at $2,000 to $3,000 [2].
- **Insurance:** HomeGuide notes your homeowners premium will likely rise [1].

## Cheaper alternatives

For someone who can sit and transfer, a stair lift costs a fraction of an elevator. For a wheelchair user going up a few feet, a vertical platform lift may work. Moving the bedroom and a full bath to the first floor is another option to price.

## DIY or hire a pro?

Hire licensed elevator professionals only.

## Who can help pay

Few programs pay for a full elevator, but some can help.

- **Medicare** does not cover home elevators.
- **Medicaid waivers** sometimes fund large home changes, but caps are often lower than elevator costs.
- **VA housing grants** (SAH and SHA) for severe service-connected disabilities can go toward large home changes.
- **State housing finance agencies** sometimes offer low-interest accessibility loans.
- **Tax deduction:** The IRS says elevators generally add value to a home. You can count as a medical expense only the part of the cost that is more than the increase in your home's value [3]. Ask a tax pro and get an appraisal.

## Bottom line

Budget $30,000 to $60,000 for a two-stop elevator in an existing home, and less if a shaftless model fits. Price a stair lift, platform lift and first-floor living plan before you commit.

faq.q: Which ramp material is cheapest?

body_md:
A ramp is often the first change a family makes when someone starts using a wheelchair, scooter or walker. Cost depends mostly on one thing: how high your entry is, because that decides how long the ramp must be.

## Wheelchair ramp cost at a glance

- **Angi** reports an average install of **$2,294**, with most projects between **$1,123 and $3,588**, based on 860 projects [1].
- **Angi** and **HomeGuide** both list **$100 to $250 per linear foot** installed [1] [2].
- **HomeAdvisor** lists ramp building at **$1,000 to $3,000**, or $100 to $200 per linear foot [3].

The sources broadly agree here.

| Ramp size (length x rise) | Typical cost | Source |
|---|---|---|
| 6 ft x 6 in | $600 – $1,000 | Angi [1] |
| 12 ft x 12 in | $1,200 – $2,500 | Angi [1] |
| 24 ft x 24 in | $2,400 – $5,000 | Angi [1] |
| 36+ ft x 36+ in | $3,600 – $7,500 | Angi [1] |

## How long does your ramp need to be?

The common guideline is a 1:12 slope, which means one foot of ramp for every inch of rise. Measure from the ground to the top of the threshold. Three steps at 7 inches each make a 21-inch rise, which calls for about 21 feet of ramp. Long ramps also need flat landings to rest and turn.

HomeGuide says permanent ramps should be at least 36 inches wide between handrails, and recommends 42 inches for homes [2].

## Aluminum vs. wood vs. concrete

| Material | Cost per linear foot, installed | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Wood | $100 – $250 | Can be built to match a porch; needs sealing and board repairs |
| Modular aluminum | $130 – $225 | Bolts together, can be moved or resold, low upkeep |
| Composite | $150 – $200 | Low upkeep, more rot resistant |
| Steel | $200 – $250 | Strong; DIY install possible |
| Concrete | $200 – $250 | Most permanent; hardest to change later |

All per-foot prices are from HomeGuide [2].

### Modular aluminum

Modular aluminum ramps come in sections that bolt together. They go up in a day or two, need no digging in many cases, and can be removed if needs change. Angi lists modular ramps at **$1,500 to $4,000** [1]. They are also the usual choice for renting, which HomeGuide lists at about **$80 to $200 or more per month** [2].

### Wood

Wood ramps can blend with the house and are easy for local carpenters to build. They need sealing and board replacement over time. Angi lists yearly upkeep for ramps at $50 to $300 [1].

### Concrete

Concrete lasts the longest but costs the most to build and change. Fixr notes a concrete ramp with railings averages about **$6,000** [4]. Handrails for concrete ramps cost extra [2].

## Other costs

- **Handrails:** $20 to $50 per linear foot [1].
- **Non-slip surface:** $5 to $20 per foot [1].
- **Permits:** $50 to $300, and some areas require inspections [1].
- **Labor:** $50 to $100 per hour, or $50 to $120 per linear foot [1].

## DIY or hire a pro?

Angi estimates DIY materials at **$500 to $2,000**, plus $50 to $300 for tools [1]. A short, straight wood ramp is within reach for an experienced builder. Long ramps, turns, landings and concrete work are better left to pros. A ramp that is too steep is a fall waiting to happen.

## Who can help pay

Ramps are among the most commonly funded home changes.

- **Area Agencies on Aging** and **nonprofit repair groups** often build ramps for free or at low cost for older adults.
- **Centers for Independent Living** may build ramps or lend modular sections.
- **Medicaid waivers** frequently cover ramps for people who qualify for home care.
- **VA:** The HISA grant lists permanent ramps as a covered change. It does not cover portable ramps [5].
- **USDA Section 504**, **city CDBG** and **state assistive technology** programs may help.
- **Tax deduction:** The IRS lists entrance and exit ramps among disability changes that usually do not add home value [6].

## Bottom line

Measure your rise, multiply by 12 to get the length in inches, and budget about $100 to $250 per foot. Ask your local aging agency or Center for Independent Living about free ramp programs first.

title: How Much Do Threshold Ramps Cost in 2026?
meta_description: Threshold ramps cost about $50 to $230 each to buy in 2026, and up to about $500 with installation. Compare rubber vs aluminum and pick the right rise height.
short: Threshold ramps for doorways and sliding-door tracks usually cost $50 to $230 each, and most people install them without a contractor.
cost_drivers: Rise height: taller sills need longer, pricier ramps
Material: rubber, aluminum or plastic modular
Width, especially for wide exterior doors

diy: Usually DIY-friendly. Rubber ramps sit in place without drilling and can be trimmed around door jambs. Make sure the ramp sits flat with no gap or lip at either edge, and that it does not block the door from closing.

faq.q: What is a threshold ramp?
faq.a: A short wedge-shaped ramp that bridges a small rise, such as a raised door sill, a sliding-door track or a step-down between rooms. Most cover rises of a few inches.

faq.q: Rubber or aluminum: which is better?
faq.a: Rubber ramps are heavy, grippy, need no drilling and conform to uneven floors. Handi-Ramp rates its rubber models to 850 pounds. Aluminum ramps are lighter and easier to move, and some have adjustable legs for uneven sills.

faq.q: How much does a pro charge to install one?
faq.a: HomeGuide lists threshold ramps at $50 to $450 each and Angi at $50 to $500, which includes some professional installs. Many people skip the installer because most ramps simply set in place.

faq.q: What rise height do I need?
faq.a: Measure from the floor to the top of the sill on the side you will roll up from. Buy a ramp rated for that rise; for example, EZ-ACCESS sells aluminum modular ramps in steps from under 1 inch up to about 6 inches of rise.

body_md:
Small lips at doorways cause a lot of trouble. A raised sill, a sliding-door track or a half-inch step between rooms can catch a walker wheel, stop a wheelchair or trip someone who shuffles. A threshold ramp smooths that bump for not much money.

## Threshold ramp cost at a glance

- **HomeGuide** lists threshold ramps at **$50 to $450** each [1].
- **Angi** lists them at **$50 to $500** [2].
- We checked one retailer's EZ-ACCESS line in October 2026. Aluminum modular threshold ramps ran from **$54** for under 1.25 inches of rise to **$217** for about 6 inches. Rubber models ran about **$120 to $230** [3].

The higher ends of the HomeGuide and Angi ranges include bigger ramps and professional fitting.

| Ramp | Rise | Price (Oct 2026) |
|---|---|---|
| Aluminum modular | 0.75 – 1.25 in | $54 |
| Aluminum modular | 1.75 – 2.25 in | $99 |
| Aluminum modular | 2.75 – 3.25 in | $122 |
| Aluminum modular | 3.75 – 4.25 in | $143 |
| Aluminum modular | 5.75 – 6.25 in | $217 |
| Rubber portable, 40 in wide | 1.5 in | about $120 – $132 |
| Rubber portable, 43 in wide | 2.5 in | about $210 – $214 |

Prices above are from MobilityMart's EZ-ACCESS listings [3]. Retail prices change often.

## Rubber vs. aluminum

### Rubber

Rubber ramps are heavy and very grippy. Handi-Ramp says they install without drilling, conform to uneven surfaces and can be notched around door jambs. It rates its rubber models up to 850 pounds [4]. They work well at front doors and between rooms where the ramp will stay put.

### Aluminum

Aluminum ramps are lighter and easier to move. Handi-Ramp notes some have adjustable legs for uneven sills, and raised-button surfaces for grip in wet weather [4]. They are a good choice when you need to take the ramp along or move it between doors.

### Plastic modular

Some plastic modular ramps lock together and are made for very small rises, often only an inch or two.

## How to choose the right ramp

1. **Measure the rise.** Measure from the floor to the top of the sill, on the side where the chair or walker will start.
2. **Measure the width.** Most interior doors take a ramp about 32 to 36 inches wide. Patio doors and front doors may need wider.
3. **Check the door swing.** Make sure the door still opens and closes over the ramp.
4. **Check both edges.** The low edge should sit flat on the floor with no lip. The top edge should meet the sill without a gap.
5. **Think about who uses it.** A power chair is heavy. Check the weight rating.

For rises over a few inches, a threshold ramp gets steep. At that point a longer modular ramp may be safer. See our wheelchair ramp cost guide for those.

## DIY or hire a pro?

Most threshold ramps are DIY. Many simply sit in place. Some aluminum models screw down for a firm fit. A pro is useful when the sill is uneven, the floor is damaged, or the ramp must be built into a deck or porch. Permits are not normally needed for a removable threshold ramp.

## Who can help pay

Threshold ramps are cheap, but help is still out there.

- **State assistive technology programs** often lend or reuse small ramps and let you try before you buy.
- **Centers for Independent Living** can advise on ramp type and sometimes supply one.
- **Area Agencies on Aging** and **nonprofit repair groups** may add threshold ramps during a home safety visit.
- **Medicaid waivers** can cover small home changes for people who qualify.
- **Tax deduction:** The IRS lists changes to the areas in front of entrances and exits among disability home changes that can count as medical expenses [5].

## Bottom line

Expect to spend $50 to $230 on a threshold ramp that fits your rise. Measure carefully, choose rubber for a ramp that stays put or aluminum for one you move, and check with your state assistive technology program before buying.

title: How Much Does It Cost to Widen a Doorway in 2026?
meta_description: Widening a doorway for a wheelchair costs about $700 to $2,500 per door in 2026, and up to $3,000 for wide or load-bearing openings. See drivers and funding.
short: Widening one doorway for a wheelchair usually costs $700 to $2,500, with load-bearing walls and wide entry doors at the top.
cost_drivers: Load-bearing wall that needs a new header or engineer
Target width: 32, 34, 36 or 40+ inches
Light switches, outlets, pipes or ducts in the wall
New door, trim, drywall and paint
Door type: swing, pocket, sliding or automatic
diy: Possible for a skilled DIYer on an interior, non-load-bearing wall with nothing in it. Angi puts DIY materials at $200 to $600. Hire a pro for load-bearing walls, wiring or plumbing in the wall, or any doubt about code.

faq.q: How wide should a doorway be for a wheelchair?
faq.a: Angi notes 32 inches as the minimum ADA clear width and 36 inches as preferred for power chairs.

faq.q: Is there a cheaper option than widening a door?
faq.a: Sometimes. Offset or swing-clear hinges move the door out of the opening and can add a little clear width. Removing the door and using a curtain is another low-cost option for some rooms.

faq.q: Do I need a permit to widen a doorway?
faq.a: Often, especially if the wall is load-bearing. Angi lists permits and fees at $50 to $300.

faq.q: How long does it take?
faq.a: Angi says a pro often finishes in one to three days, while DIY may take a full weekend or longer.

body_md:
Many older homes have bathroom and bedroom doors only 24 to 30 inches wide. That is too tight for most wheelchairs and many walkers. Widening a door is one of the most useful changes for someone who needs a mobility aid.

## Doorway widening cost at a glance

The sources we checked agree on the general range.

- **Angi** reports a national average of **$1,200**, with most jobs between **$50 and $3,000** [1].
- **HomeAdvisor** lists **$700 to $2,500 per door** [2].
- **Fixr** lists **$300 to $2,500** [3].

The very low end of Angi's range ($50) likely covers simple jobs like removing trim or a door stop, not true widening. For real widening, plan on at least a few hundred dollars.

| Target width | Typical cost | Source |
|---|---|---|
| 32 in (minimum ADA width) | $300 – $1,000 | Angi [1] |
| 34 in | $400 – $1,300 | Angi [1] |
| 36 in (preferred for power chairs) | $600 – $2,500 | Angi [1] |
| 40 in+ (main entry or custom) | $1,200 – $3,000 | Angi [1] |

## What drives the price

### Load-bearing walls

This is the big one. If the wall holds up the floor or roof above, the opening needs a new, longer header. That may mean an engineer. Angi lists structural changes, including headers, at **$300 to $1,000**, and structural engineers at **$100 to $250 per hour** [1].

### What is inside the wall

Light switches, outlets, pipes and heating ducts near the door must be moved. Angi lists utility relocation at **$100 to $800** [1].

### Finishing work

After the wall is cut, you need a new door and frame, drywall patching, trim and paint. Angi puts materials and tools at $100 to $600 and finishing at $100 to $600 [1].

### Door type

A standard swing door is simplest. A pocket or sliding door saves floor space but adds cost. Automatic openers add more [1].

## Line-item costs

| Component | Range |
|---|---|
| Materials and tools | $100 – $600 |
| Labor | $200 – $1,200 |
| Permits and fees | $50 – $300 |
| Finishing (paint, trim, hardware) | $100 – $600 |
| Structural changes | $300 – $1,000 |
| Moving wiring, switches, pipes or vents | $100 – $800 |

All from Angi [1].

## Lower-cost options to try first

- **Offset (swing-clear) hinges** let the door swing fully out of the opening, which can gain a little clear width without cutting the wall.
- **Remove the door stop and trim** to gain a fraction of an inch.
- **Take the door off** a closet or low-privacy room.

An occupational therapist can measure the actual chair or walker and tell you whether hinges will do or the wall must be cut.

## Plan the whole path

A wide bathroom door does not help if the hallway outside is too narrow to turn into it. Fixr lists hallway widening without structural change at $800 to $1,400, and with structural change at $30,000 to $40,000 [4]. Measure the full route from bed to bathroom before you start.

## DIY or hire a pro?

Angi says DIY materials run about $200 to $600, and the job may take a full weekend or longer [1]. Angi recommends a pro for structural changes, utility moves or unclear code rules [1]. If you do not know whether the wall is load-bearing, do not cut it.

## Who can help pay

- **Medicaid waivers** often cover doorway widening as a home change.
- **VA HISA grants** cover medically needed changes for getting into and out of the home and reaching the bathroom, within lifetime limits of $6,800 or $2,000 [5].
- **Area Agencies on Aging**, **Centers for Independent Living** and **nonprofit repair groups** can help find funding or crews.
- **USDA Section 504**, **city CDBG** and **state housing finance agency** programs fund repairs for eligible owners.
- **Tax deduction:** The IRS lists widened doorways and hallways among disability changes that usually do not add home value, so the full reasonable cost can count [6].

## Bottom line

Budget $700 to $2,500 per door, and more for load-bearing walls or extra-wide entries. Try offset hinges first, measure the whole route, and bundle several doors into one job to save on trip and permit costs.

title: How Much Do Lever Door Handles and Easy-Use Faucets Cost in 2026?
meta_description: Lever door handles cost under $100 each and about $100 to $350 installed in 2026; single-lever faucets run $200 to $680 installed. See DIY tips and funding.

faq.q: Why are lever handles better than knobs?
faq.a: Knobs need a strong grip and a wrist twist. Levers can be pushed down with a fist, palm or elbow, which helps people with arthritis, weak hands or full hands.

faq.q: How much does it cost to replace a doorknob with a lever?
faq.a: Angi says most levers cost under $100 and can be installed yourself. HomeGuide lists professional doorknob replacement at $100 to $250, with an average of $150.

faq.q: Are touchless faucets worth it?
faq.a: They can help people with very weak hands or memory issues. HomeGuide lists touchless faucets at $150 to $600 before installation.

faq.q: Can I deduct lever handles on my taxes?
faq.a: The IRS lists modified door hardware among disability home changes that can count as medical expenses, subject to the 7.5 percent of income floor.

body_md:
Round doorknobs and twist faucets are hard to use with arthritis, a weak grip or a stroke. Levers fix that. You can push a lever with a closed fist, a palm or even an elbow. This is one of the cheapest changes you can make, and it helps everyone in the house.

## Cost at a glance

| Item | Typical cost | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Lever door set (hardware) | Under $100 for most | Angi [1] |
| Pro install of door hardware, per door | $140 – $350 | Angi [1] |
| Doorknob replacement, installed | $100 – $250 (avg. $150) | HomeGuide [2] |
| Kitchen knobs to levers | $150 – $350 | Fixr [3] |
| Kitchen faucet, installed | $250 – $600 | HomeGuide [4] |
| Bathroom faucet, installed | $230 – $680 | HomeGuide [4] |
| Touchless faucet (part only) | $150 – $600 | HomeGuide [4] |

## Lever door handles

Angi says most door levers cost **less than $100** and are easy to install yourself [1]. It lists professional installation of door knobs at **$140 to $350 per door**, and installing a lever is the same kind of job [1]. HomeGuide puts doorknob replacement at **$100 to $250**, with a national average of **$150**, a low of $75 and a high of $400 [2]. In HomeGuide's numbers, labor is about half the bill [2].

A standard swap into existing holes takes about 30 minutes [2]. Doing every door in one visit cuts the cost per door, since many pros charge a minimum visit fee.

### Which type to buy

- **Passage levers** have no lock. Use them for halls and closets. They are the cheapest [2].
- **Privacy levers** lock with a push button. Use them for bathrooms and bedrooms. Pick one that unlocks from outside with a simple tool, so a helper can get in during an emergency.
- **Keyed levers** are for exterior doors. Consider a keypad lever so no one has to work a small key.

## Easy-use faucets

A single-lever faucet lets you set water flow and heat with one motion. A pull-down sprayer helps fill pots without lifting them. A touchless faucet turns on with a wave.

HomeGuide lists faucet prices before installation [4]:

- Single-handle: $40 to $500
- Pull-down: $80 to $700
- Touchless: $150 to $600
- Bathroom sink faucets: $70 to $250

Installed totals run about **$250 to $600** in the kitchen and **$230 to $680** in the bathroom [4]. Labor alone averages about $185 [4].

### Safety tip: hot water

Easier faucets make it easier to get hot water fast. If the person has reduced feeling in their hands, ask the plumber about an anti-scald valve or lowering the water heater setting. Fixr lists anti-scald controls at $80 to $300 [3].

## DIY or hire a pro?

**Levers:** Usually DIY. Take the old knob to the store, or measure the backset and door thickness, to make sure the new lever fits the existing holes.

**Faucets:** HomeGuide says a straight swap is DIY-friendly, but upgrades that need new holes or more plumbing usually need a pro [4]. Old, stuck shutoff valves are a common reason to call a plumber.

No permit is needed for lever swaps. A simple faucet swap normally does not need one either. Check local rules if valves or supply lines are changed.

## Who can help pay

- **Area Agencies on Aging** and **nonprofit repair groups** often swap knobs for levers during home safety visits.
- **State assistive technology programs** and **Centers for Independent Living** can suggest products and sometimes provide them.
- **Medicaid waivers** may cover small home changes as part of a home care plan.
- **Tax deduction:** The IRS lists modified door hardware and modified fixtures among disability changes that can count as medical expenses [5].

## Bottom line

Lever handles cost under $100 each and take minutes to install, so do every door that matters. Pair them with a single-lever faucet in the kitchen and bathroom for one of the best-value safety upgrades in the home.

faq.q: How much does it cost to install a motion sensor light?
faq.a: Angi puts first-time installation at about $350 to $500, with an average near $425. Fixr's aging-in-place guide gives a similar $350 to $500 for sensor light installation.

faq.q: Can I install motion lights myself?
faq.a: Battery and solar lights, yes. Angi estimates DIY cost at about $150 to $300. Hardwired lights should go to an electrician.

faq.q: Where should night lights go?
faq.a: Along the path from bed to bathroom, in the bathroom itself, at the top and bottom of stairs, and at entry doors. Motion-activated lights avoid fumbling for switches.

faq.q: Does better lighting really prevent falls?
faq.a: Poor lighting is a common fall hazard in homes. Lighting the path to the bathroom at night is one of the simplest changes an occupational therapist will suggest.

body_md:
Many falls happen at night, on the way to the bathroom, when the house is dark. Older eyes need more light and take longer to adjust to darkness. Good lighting is one of the cheapest and most effective safety changes you can make.

## Lighting upgrade costs at a glance

| Upgrade | Typical cost | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Motion sensor light, installed | $350 – $500 (avg. about $425) | Angi [1] |
| Sensor light installation | $350 – $500 | Fixr [2] |
| Motion-sensing lights (accessibility project) | $200 – $600 | Angi [3] |
| Outdoor sensor lights | $300 – $400 | Fixr [2] |
| Bathroom lighting installation | $20 – $100 | Fixr [2] |
| Lower light switches | $20 – $100 | Fixr [4] |
| Full outdoor lighting upgrade | $2,000 – $6,000 | Angi [3] |

The sources agree well on motion lights. Angi and Fixr both land at $350 to $500 for a typical install [1] [2].

## Motion sensor lights

Motion lights turn on when someone walks by and off after a set time. Indoors they light halls and stairs. Outdoors they light walkways, steps and the driveway.

Angi lists fixture prices before installation [1]:

- Hardwired: $15 to $200 per light
- Battery-powered: $20 to $100 per light
- Solar-powered: $25 to $300 per light

Installed, a motion floodlight runs $250 to $600, and a decorative motion fixture $250 to $350 [1]. Electricians charge about $50 to $150 per hour [1].

## Night lights and path lights

Plug-in and battery night lights are the cheapest upgrade of all. Motion-activated models turn on only when needed. Many families place them:

- Beside the bed
- Along the hall to the bathroom
- Inside the bathroom, near the toilet
- At the top and bottom of stairs
- Near entry doors

Fixr's low figure of $20 to $100 for bathroom lighting reflects this kind of simple fix [2].

## Switches people can reach and see

Lighted rocker switches are easier to find in the dark and easier to press than small toggles. Fixr lists lowering light switches, which helps wheelchair users, at $20 to $100 [4]. Smart switches and smart bulbs let someone turn on lights by voice or by phone.

## Brighter rooms

Older adults often need much more light to read labels and see edges. Ask an electrician about adding fixtures in dim kitchens, stairways and closets. Fixr lists lighting upgrades for people with low vision at $350 to $500 [4].

## Outdoor lighting

Lighting the path from the car to the door matters as much as indoor light. Angi lists a full outdoor lighting upgrade at $2,000 to $6,000 [3], but one or two motion floodlights over the entry and driveway cover the biggest risks for much less.

## DIY or hire a pro?

Angi says battery and solar lights are fine for DIY and advises against DIY hardwired installs [1]. It estimates DIY cost at about **$150 to $300**, compared with about **$425** for a pro [1].

Hardwired fixtures and new switches may need an electrical permit in some areas. A licensed electrician will know the local rules.

## Who can help pay

- **Area Agencies on Aging** and **nonprofit repair groups** often install night lights and lighting fixes during home safety visits.
- **State assistive technology programs** can show lighting products and smart-home tools for people with low vision.
- **Medicaid waivers** may cover home changes that support safety at home.
- **City CDBG repair programs** sometimes fix unsafe wiring and lighting for eligible owners.
- **Tax deduction:** The IRS lists moving or modifying electrical outlets and fixtures among disability changes that can count as medical expenses [5].

## Bottom line

Start with $20 to $50 worth of motion night lights along the bed-to-bathroom path tonight. Then budget about $350 to $500 per hardwired motion light for stairs, entries and the driveway.

body_md:
Slick floors cause many falls, especially in bathrooms and kitchens where floors get wet. Replacing glossy tile or worn vinyl with a slip-resistant surface can make a big difference. It also gives you a chance to remove raised thresholds and loose rugs.

## Non-slip flooring cost at a glance

- **Angi** lists nonslip flooring at **$3 to $22 per square foot** [1].
- **Fixr** lists anti-skid bathroom tile at **$4,500 to $8,000** per bathroom and non-slip kitchen flooring at **$6,400 to $11,000** [2].
- **HomeGuide** prices bathroom floors by material, from **$2 per square foot** for sheet vinyl to **$50** for porcelain tile [3].

Fixr's project totals seem high for a small bathroom and likely include tear-out, subfloor work and larger rooms. Use the per-foot numbers to check any quote.

| Material | Installed cost per sq ft | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Sheet vinyl | $2 – $7 | HomeGuide [3] |
| Luxury vinyl plank (LVP) | $4 – $16 | HomeGuide [3] |
| Ceramic tile | $12 – $40 | HomeGuide [3] |
| Porcelain tile | $15 – $50 | HomeGuide [3] |
| Nonslip flooring, general | $3 – $22 | Angi [1] |

For a 40-square-foot bathroom floor, that works out to roughly $80 to $280 in sheet vinyl or $160 to $640 in LVP before tear-out and repairs, using HomeGuide's ranges [3].

## Choosing a floor that grips

### Vinyl and luxury vinyl plank

Vinyl resists water and feels softer and warmer underfoot than tile. Many products have a textured surface. It is often the best value for aging in place.

### Tile

Tile lasts a long time, but glossy tile gets slick when wet. Matte or textured tile, and small mosaic tile with more grout lines, give better grip. HomeGuide notes that textured finishes help prevent slips in small bathrooms [3]. Ask the store for the tile's wet slip rating.

### Epoxy and other coatings

HomeGuide warns epoxy can be slippery unless an anti-slip additive is used [3]. The same goes for polished concrete.

### Floors to avoid

Deep-pile carpet can catch walker feet and wheelchair wheels. Loose throw rugs are a top trip hazard.

## Hidden costs

- **Tear-out.** Removing old tile is slow, messy work.
- **Subfloor repair.** Old bathrooms often have soft spots near the toilet or tub.
- **Thresholds.** Matching floor heights between rooms removes trip edges. Ask your installer to plan flat transitions.
- **Moving the toilet.** Bathroom floors usually require pulling the toilet and resetting it.

## Low-cost fixes

Before buying new floors, try the cheap stuff:

- Remove throw rugs. Fixr lists throw rug removal as an aging-in-place task at $150 to $250 [2].
- Add a bedside safety mat. Fixr lists $80 to $200 [2].
- Put non-slip strips or a mat in the tub or shower.
- Use rug tape or rug pads for rugs you keep.
- Wipe up spills right away and use non-slip shoes at home.

## DIY or hire a pro?

Click-lock vinyl plank is a popular DIY floor in dry rooms. In bathrooms, water resistance at the edges matters, so many people hire a pro. Tile work is labor-heavy and best left to a skilled installer. A permit is not usually needed for flooring alone, but check if the subfloor or plumbing is changed.

## Who can help pay

- **Area Agencies on Aging** and **nonprofit repair groups** often fix trip hazards and slippery floors for low-income seniors.
- **Medicaid waivers** may cover floor changes that support safety at home.
- **USDA Section 504** grants can fix health and safety hazards for very-low-income rural owners 62 and older [4].
- **City CDBG** and **state housing finance agency** repair programs may help eligible owners.
- **Tax deduction:** Flooring changes made for a medical reason may count only if they do not add home value, and only the medical part counts. Ask a tax pro.

## Bottom line

Budget about $3 to $22 per square foot for slip-resistant flooring, with vinyl at the low end. Fix rugs and tub mats first, then replace the bathroom floor if it is slick when wet.
