body_md:
Stairs are one of the riskiest places in any home. A sturdy handrail, ideally on both sides, is one of the simplest ways to make them safer. It costs far less than a stair lift and helps everyone in the family.

## Handrail cost at a glance

- **HomeGuide** lists stair railings at **$500 to $1,500** installed for a typical 25-foot wood project, and notes that wall-mounted rails fall at the low end of prices [1].
- **Fixr** lists stair handrails for aging in place at **$800 to $1,200**, and handrails beside outdoor steps at **$700 to $1,200** [2]. Its disability remodel guide lists **$350 to $1,200** [3].
- **HomeAdvisor** lists railing installation at **$1,000 to $2,500** [4].

The ranges overlap well around $500 to $1,500 for a basic rail. HomeAdvisor's range runs higher and likely includes full railings.

| Material (indoor) | Cost per linear foot, installed | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Wood | $20 – $60 | HomeGuide [1] |
| Aluminum | $50 – $200 | HomeGuide [1] |
| Stainless steel | $50 – $250 | HomeGuide [1] |
| Wrought iron | $65 – $135 | HomeGuide [1] |

## Indoor stair handrails

A wall-mounted handrail is a round or oval rail held by brackets screwed into the wall studs. It is the cheapest kind of rail. HomeGuide says installers charge about $300 to $1,000 for an average 25-foot project, or $60 to $100 per hour [1].

If the open side of your stairs has an old, wobbly railing with balusters, fixing or replacing that costs more. HomeGuide lists balusters at about $1,200 to $1,500 on average [1].

## Outdoor handrails

Outdoor rails beside porch steps and walkways have to handle weather and be anchored into concrete, brick or wood. HomeGuide puts outdoor handrails at an average of **$700** per 5-foot section, with a range of **$275 to $1,150**, or about **$50 to $230 per linear foot** [5].

| Outdoor rail length | Low-end total | High-end total |
|---|---|---|
| 5 ft (3 to 5 porch steps) | $250 – $400 | $700 – $1,150 |
| 10 ft | $500 – $800 | $1,400 – $2,300 |
| 20 ft | $1,000 – $1,600 | $2,800 – $4,600 |

From HomeGuide [5].

HomeGuide lists aluminum and steel at about $40 to $60 per foot, vinyl at $25 to $45, and wrought iron at $50 to $120 [5]. Concrete anchoring costs more than attaching to wood framing [5].

## What makes a handrail safe

HomeGuide lists some common code basics [5]:

- Typical residential rail height of about **36 inches**
- A graspable rail **1.25 to 2 inches** across
- Balusters no more than **4 inches** apart

For aging in place, also look for:

- A rail on **both sides** of the stairs
- A rail that runs the **full length** of the stairs, past the top and bottom steps
- Brackets that do not catch the hand as it slides
- A color that contrasts with the wall so it is easy to see

## DIY or hire a pro?

HomeGuide lists basic DIY outdoor rail kits at $50 to $150 for a 5-foot section [5]. Indoor wall-mounted rails are a fair DIY project if you can find studs and set brackets level. The rail must hold a falling adult, so if you are unsure, hire a handyperson or carpenter. Outdoor rails in concrete are best left to pros.

Permits for outdoor railings run $50 to $300 where required [5].

## Who can help pay

- **Area Agencies on Aging** and **nonprofit repair groups** often install handrails as part of free home safety repairs.
- **Medicaid waivers** may cover handrails as a home change.
- **USDA Section 504** grants, **city CDBG** programs and **Centers for Independent Living** can help eligible owners.
- **VA HISA grants** can help veterans with medically needed changes to get into and out of the home.
- **Tax deduction:** The IRS lists railings and modified stairways among disability changes that usually do not add home value [6].

## Bottom line

Budget about $500 to $1,500 for a solid wall-mounted rail on an indoor staircase, and about $275 to $1,150 for a short outdoor rail. Put rails on both sides wherever you can.

faq.a: HomeGuide lists converting a bedroom or office into a bathroom at $20,000 to $38,000 for 100 to 150 square feet.

body_md:
When stairs become hard, many families move daily life to the first floor. That usually means a bedroom and a bathroom with a shower on the main level. Cost depends on one big choice: convert space you already have, or build new.

## First-floor conversion cost at a glance

| Project | Typical cost | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Convert existing space into a bathroom | $5,000 – $25,000 | HomeGuide [1] |
| Small half-bath conversion (15 – 20 sq ft) | $3,000 – $5,000 | HomeGuide [1] |
| Three-quarter bath conversion (25 – 40 sq ft) | $5,000 – $10,000 | HomeGuide [1] |
| Convert bedroom or office into bathroom | $20,000 – $38,000 | HomeGuide [1] |
| Garage into bathroom | $20,000 – $30,000 | HomeGuide [1] |
| New bathroom addition | $20,000 – $75,000 | HomeGuide [1] |
| New primary bedroom and bath addition | $37,500 – $117,000 (avg. $103,300) | Angi [2] |
| Bedroom remodel | $5,000 – $10,000 | Fixr [3] |

HomeAdvisor's range for building an addition is lower, at **$10,000 to $75,000 or more** [4]. Angi's top range for a bedroom and bath addition reaches **$150,000** [2]. The gap reflects very different project sizes.

## Option 1: convert space you already have

Many homes have a den, dining room, office or family room on the first floor that can become a bedroom. Often the bedroom part is easy: add a door, a closet and good lighting.

The bathroom is the costly part. HomeGuide says converting existing space into a bathroom runs **$5,000 to $25,000**, or about **$200 to $250 per square foot** [1]. It also says a conversion can save nearly half compared with an addition [1].

### Spaces that cost less

Spaces close to existing plumbing cost less. HomeGuide lists a closet or under-stair space at $3,000 to $7,500 and a laundry room at $7,500 to $16,000 [1]. A laundry room already has a drain and water lines.

### Spaces that cost more

A bedroom or office conversion runs $20,000 to $38,000, and a garage $20,000 to $30,000 [1], because drain lines must be run farther and floors often need work. HomeGuide lists rough-in plumbing alone at $450 to $1,800 [1].

## Option 2: build an addition

If there is no spare room, an addition adds a new suite on the ground floor. Angi reports a national average of **$103,300** for a primary bedroom and bath addition, with most spending **$37,500 to $117,000**, or about **$80 to $220 per square foot** [2]. Additions need a foundation, framing, roofing and often an architect and engineer. Angi lists permits averaging about **$900** [2].

## Design the space for the long run

Whichever route you choose, build it so it will still work if needs grow:

- A doorway at least 32 inches clear, and 36 inches if a power chair is possible
- A curbless or low-threshold shower with a seat and grab bars
- Blocking in the walls for future grab bars
- A comfort-height toilet with room beside it for a helper
- Lever handles, good lighting and non-slip floors
- A clear path from bed to bathroom

An occupational therapist or a Certified Aging-in-Place Specialist (CAPS) can review plans before you build.

## Budget for surprises

HomeGuide suggests setting aside 10 to 20 percent of the budget for unforeseen issues, and notes older homes may need extra plumbing or electrical work [1].

## DIY or hire a pro?

Hire a licensed contractor and pull permits. Labor is about half of bathroom project cost, according to HomeGuide [1], so families sometimes save by painting or doing cleanup themselves.

## Who can help pay

- **Medicaid waivers** can cover accessible bathroom changes, though caps are often below the cost of a full conversion.
- **VA grants** such as HISA cover bathroom access for eligible veterans, and larger SAH and SHA grants cover bigger projects for severe service-connected disabilities.
- **USDA Section 504** loans of up to $40,000 at a fixed 1 percent rate, plus grants up to $10,000 for owners 62 and older, help very-low-income rural owners [5].
- **City CDBG**, **state housing finance agency** and **nonprofit repair** programs may help with accessible bathrooms.
- **Tax deduction:** Bathroom changes for a disability can count as medical expenses, but an addition may raise home value, which reduces the deductible part under IRS rules [6].

## Bottom line

If you have a usable first-floor room near plumbing, a conversion often lands between $5,000 and $38,000. A new suite addition usually costs far more. Price both before deciding to move.

body_md:
A kitchen that worked for decades can become hard to use with a walker, a wheelchair or weak hands. Upper cabinets get out of reach, knobs are hard to turn, and standing at the stove gets tiring. Some fixes cost a few hundred dollars. Others mean a full remodel.

## Accessible kitchen costs at a glance

| Change | Typical cost | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Kitchen knobs to levers | $150 – $350 | Fixr [1] |
| Shallow sink addition | $200 – $3,000 | Fixr [1] |
| Accessible countertop | $600 – $2,000 | Fixr [2] |
| Wheelchair-accessible sink | $450 – $800 | Fixr [2] |
| Kitchen cabinets and sink installation | $1,500 – $8,500 | Angi [3] |
| Lowering cabinets | $1,500 – $8,500 | HomeAdvisor [4] |
| Lower-height cabinets | $4,000 – $9,000 | Fixr [2] |
| Cabinet lifting system | $5,000 – $9,000 | Fixr [2] |
| Cabinet and counter lowering | $15,000 – $20,000 | Fixr [1] |
| Full accessible kitchen remodel | $13,000 – $38,000 | Angi [3], HomeAdvisor [4] |
| New accessible kitchen layout | $9,000 – $50,000 | Fixr [1] |

## Where the sources disagree

The cost to lower cabinets and counters varies a lot by source. HomeAdvisor lists **$1,500 to $8,500** [4], Fixr's disability guide lists **$4,000 to $9,000** for lower cabinets [2], and Fixr's aging-in-place guide lists **$15,000 to $20,000** for lowering cabinets and counters [1]. The low end likely covers a section of cabinets. The high end covers most of a kitchen, with new countertops. Ask contractors to price the exact run of cabinets you need.

## Low-cost changes

- **Lever or D-shaped handles** on cabinets and drawers. Easier for stiff hands than small knobs.
- **Single-lever or touchless faucet.** One motion sets heat and flow.
- **Pull-out shelves and lazy Susans** in base cabinets, so no one has to kneel and reach.
- **Better task lighting** under upper cabinets.
- **Front-control cooktop** or stove knob covers, so no one reaches over hot burners.
- **Moving everyday items** to shelves between hip and shoulder height. Free.

## Mid-range changes

### A seated work area

A section of counter at about table height, with open space below, lets someone prep food sitting down. Fixr lists accessible countertops at $600 to $2,000 [2].

### Roll-under sink

A sink with open knee space lets a wheelchair user pull in. Fixr lists a wheelchair-accessible sink at $450 to $800 [2]. Cover or insulate the pipes so they do not burn legs.

### Lowering a run of cabinets

This is where costs rise. It may mean new countertops and moving plumbing or outlets. See the price ranges above.

## Full accessible remodel

Angi and HomeAdvisor both list a kitchen remodel that lowers cabinets and counters and widens floor space at **$13,000 to $38,000** [3] [4]. Fixr lists a new kitchen layout at $9,000 to $50,000 [1]. Common features include:

- Wider aisles for turning a wheelchair
- A wall oven at a reachable height and a side-opening door
- A side-by-side or drawer-style refrigerator
- Dishwasher raised off the floor
- Non-slip flooring

## DIY or hire a pro?

Handles, shelf kits and moving items are easy DIY tasks. Lowering counters, moving a sink or adding outlets requires a contractor, and plumbing and electrical work usually needs permits. A Certified Aging-in-Place Specialist (CAPS) or occupational therapist can help plan heights for the actual user.

## Who can help pay

- **VA HISA grant:** The VA lists access to kitchen sinks and counters, such as lowering them, as a covered change [5]. Lifetime limits are $6,800 for service-connected cases and $2,000 for others [5].
- **Medicaid waivers** may cover kitchen changes that support independent living.
- **Centers for Independent Living** and **state assistive technology programs** can suggest products and help find funds.
- **Area Agencies on Aging** and **nonprofit repair groups** may handle smaller changes.
- **State housing finance agencies** sometimes offer accessibility loans.
- **Tax deduction:** The IRS lists lowered or modified kitchen cabinets and equipment among disability changes that usually do not add home value [6].

## Bottom line

Start with handles, a lever faucet and pull-out shelves for a few hundred dollars. Budget $1,500 to $8,500 to rework a section of cabinets and the sink, and $13,000 or more for a full accessible kitchen.

title: How Much Does an Occupational Therapist Home Safety Assessment Cost in 2026?
meta_description: A private-pay OT home safety assessment costs about $125 to $400 in 2026, and Medicare may cover it when a doctor orders therapy. See what's included.

faq.a: Medicare Part B covers medically necessary outpatient occupational therapy when a provider certifies the need; you pay 20 percent after the deductible. Under the home health benefit, homebound patients pay $0 for covered services, including OT.

faq.a: An OT-run guide from AskSAMIE puts typical in-home assessments at $125 to $400. One OT practice we checked lists general evaluations at $275 and in-home services at $110 per hour.

faq.a: Yes. An OT assesses the person's health and abilities. A Certified Aging-in-Place Specialist is a builder or designer trained to make the changes. Many families use both.

body_md:
Before spending thousands on home changes, it pays to know which changes matter most for the person who will use them. An occupational therapist (OT) can tell you. An OT home safety assessment looks at how someone moves through daily life at home and where they are likely to fall.

## OT home safety assessment cost at a glance

There is no national price list for this service, so we checked several sources. Prices are modest compared with the work they guide.

| Option | Typical cost | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Private-pay in-home OT assessment | $125 – $400 | AskSAMIE [1] |
| Private-pay OT or PT evaluation (one practice) | $275; in-home services $110 per hour | First Priority OT [2] |
| Private-pay OT (general) | "A few hundred dollars" | SeniorThrive [3] |
| Medicare Part B outpatient OT | 20% of approved amount after deductible | Medicare.gov [4] |
| Medicare home health OT (homebound) | $0 for covered services | Medicare.gov [5] |

Private prices vary by area and by how long the visit lasts [1] [3].

## What you get

AskSAMIE, a guide written with OTs, says a good assessment includes watching the person transfer in and out of chairs, bed, toilet and tub; checking walking and balance; testing reach and grip; and observing daily tasks [1]. You should get a written report with fall-risk notes and a prioritized list of changes [1].

That list might say, for example:

- Grab bars at specific heights by the toilet and in the shower
- A shower seat and handheld shower
- A raised toilet or toilet frame
- Moving the bedroom downstairs
- Removing rugs and adding lights on the path to the bathroom

## How Medicare can help

### Outpatient OT (Part B)

Medicare Part B covers medically necessary outpatient occupational therapy when a doctor or other qualified provider certifies the need [4]. After you meet the Part B deductible, you pay **20 percent** of the Medicare-approved amount [4]. Medicare says there is no yearly dollar limit on medically necessary outpatient therapy [4].

### Home health OT

If the person is homebound and a provider orders home health care, Medicare covers home health services at **$0** cost to the patient [5]. OT must start alongside skilled nursing, physical therapy or speech therapy, and can then continue on its own [5]. A home health OT often looks at home safety as part of the visits.

### What Medicare does not pay for

Medicare generally does not pay for the home changes an OT recommends, such as grab bars, ramps or stair lifts [1] [3]. Some Medicare Advantage plans include a home safety benefit; AskSAMIE reports amounts often between $500 and $2,500 per year [1]. Check your own plan.

## Private pay vs. insurance

Private-pay assessments do not need a doctor's referral and can often be scheduled faster [1]. Insurance-covered OT needs a provider's order. If your parent just left the hospital or had a fall, ask the doctor about a home health or outpatient OT referral first.

## OT vs. CAPS contractor

A Certified Aging-in-Place Specialist (CAPS) is a contractor or designer trained in aging-in-place building. SeniorThrive notes CAPS assessments are often cheaper than OT fees, and some contractors credit the fee toward the work [3]. AskSAMIE points out that CAPS pros make the changes but do not evaluate clinical needs, and suggests pairing an OT assessment with a qualified contractor [1].

## How to find an OT

- Ask the person's doctor for a referral.
- Ask the hospital discharge planner or home health agency.
- Call your local Area Agency on Aging, which may know of free or low-cost home safety programs.
- Contact a Center for Independent Living.
- Veterans can ask their VA care team.

## Who can help pay

- **Medicare** Part B outpatient OT and the home health benefit [4] [5].
- **Medicaid waivers** may include home assessments as part of planning home changes.
- **Area Agencies on Aging** sometimes offer free home safety checks.
- **VA** care teams can arrange evaluations for veterans and must document medical need for HISA grants.
- **Centers for Independent Living** can advise on accessibility.

## Bottom line

Expect to pay about $125 to $400 privately, or much less if Medicare covers OT after a provider's order. It is a small cost that can keep you from spending thousands on the wrong changes.

body_md:
A medical alert system lets someone call for help with the press of a button, even if they cannot reach a phone. Many come with automatic fall detection. For people who live alone, it is often the first safety purchase a family makes.

Unlike most items on our site, this is a monthly cost. Here is what to expect in 2026.

## Medical alert cost at a glance

- **NCOA** says monthly fees generally run **$20 to $60 or more**, with an average of about **$40** [1].
- **AARP's** 2026 top picks start at **$27.95 to $44.95 per month** [2].
- **Fixr** lists medical alert systems at **$20 to $50 per month** [3].

The sources agree well.

| Plan type | Monthly fee | Source |
|---|---|---|
| In-home, landline (four major brands) | $24.95 – $49.95 | NCOA [1] |
| Mobile GPS (four major brands) | $29.95 – $54.95 | NCOA [1] |
| Smartwatch plans | About $39.95 – $42.95, plus $159 – $199.95 for the watch | NCOA [1] |
| Fall detection add-on | Usually about $10 | AARP [2], NCOA [1] |
| One-time equipment | $0 – $200 | NCOA [1] |
| One-time activation | $25 – $100, if charged | NCOA [1] |

## In-home vs. on-the-go

### In-home systems

An in-home system has a base unit and a wearable button. It works within range of the base, usually the house and yard. NCOA lists in-home plans from four major brands at **$24.95 to $49.95** a month, and says cellular or Wi-Fi versions may cost more than landline [1].

### Mobile GPS systems

A mobile device works anywhere with cell service and can share location. NCOA lists mobile plans at **$29.95 to $54.95** a month [1]. AARP lists MobileHelp at about $29.95 for at-home and $41.95 for mobile, and Bay Alarm Medical's SOS Micro at $34.95 [2].

### Smartwatches

Some brands sell alert smartwatches. NCOA lists watches at $159 to $199.95 up front plus about $39.95 to $42.95 a month [1].

## Fall detection

Fall detection uses sensors to call for help if the wearer falls and cannot press the button. AARP says it usually costs about **$10 more per month** [2]. It lists $10 at Medical Guardian, MobileHelp and Bay Alarm Medical, $5 at LifeFone, and $8 to $16 at LifeStation [2]. No fall detection is perfect, so the wearer should still press the button when they can.

## Upfront and hidden costs

- **Equipment:** $0 to $200, paid once or spread out, per NCOA [1]. AARP notes Bay Alarm's SOS Micro has a one-time $104 equipment fee, and MobileHelp has no activation or equipment fees [2].
- **Activation:** $25 to $100 at companies that charge it [1].
- **Protection plans:** $1 to $10 a month [1].
- **Restocking fees:** up to $50 for returned leased equipment [1].
- **Contracts:** NCOA notes Bay Alarm Medical, Medical Alert and Medical Guardian have no cancellation penalty, while MobileHelp requires a three-month minimum [1].

## Yearly cost

NCOA estimates **$275 to $485 a year** for in-home landline plans and **$384 to $519** for on-the-go plans, before fall detection and promotions [1]. Paying yearly or quarterly can earn a small discount [1].

## Tips for choosing

- Pick in-home if the person rarely leaves home alone. Pick mobile if they drive, walk or shop alone.
- Ask about response time and whether the monitoring center is staffed around the clock.
- Check the device is waterproof so it can be worn in the shower, where many falls happen.
- Read the cancellation terms before you sign.

## DIY setup

Most systems are set up by the family. Plug in the base or charge the device, then press the button to test it with the monitoring center. Test monthly.

## Who can help pay

- **Medicare:** Original Medicare does not cover medical alert systems [1]. Some Medicare Advantage plans may [1] [2].
- **Medicaid waivers:** AARP reports some Medicaid waivers may offer coverage [2].
- **VA:** The VA offers free or low-cost systems to eligible veterans [1].
- **Long-term care insurance** often pays part or all of the cost, usually after a waiting period [1].
- **HSA and FSA funds** may be usable, depending on your account rules [1].
- **Area Agencies on Aging** may know of local programs that help with monthly fees.

## Bottom line

Plan on $25 to $45 a month, plus about $10 for fall detection and up to $200 up front. Compare two or three providers, and check Medicaid, VA and long-term care insurance before paying full price.
